deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German-language lecture or study notes on ancient Macedonian history. It continues the previous page, which surveys the Macedonian kings from Perdiccas II to Amyntas II (that is, Amyntas III in modern numbering, r. 393/390–370/369 BC).

The page opens with a small genealogical diagram:
- Amyntas II
- his three sons: Alexander (II), Perdiccas (III), Philipp (II)
- below Perdiccas: his son 'Amytas' (Amyntas IV); below Philipp: his son Alexander M[agnus].

The prose then narrates the following:
- Alexander II had a rival in Ptolemaeus (Ptolemy of Aloros), so the Macedonians appealed to Thebes.
- Pelopidas came, secured the king on the throne, and took young Philip to Thebes as a hostage.
- In 368 Alexander was overthrown (murdered) through Ptolemaeus.
- Pelopidas came a second time and arranged that Ptolemaeus remain regent, on the promise to keep the throne for Perdiccas and Philip.
- In 365 Ptolemaeus was murdered by Perdiccas III.

The next page continues with Perdiccas III, Pausanias, Perdiccas' death against the Illyrians in 360, and Philip II's accession and the phalanx.

There is no derivation, formula or computation to reconstruct. The bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816' notwithstanding, this folio is historical prose, apparently notes taken from a history lecture. It may not even be in Gauss's own hand.
errors: Not mathematical; only historical accuracy can be assessed.
'Amytas' in the genealogy is a slip for Amyntas (Amyntas IV, son of Perdiccas III).
'Amyntas II' follows an older numbering; modern scholarship usually calls this king Amyntas III, with his death dated 370/369 BC.

Dates are broadly consistent with standard chronology: Alexander II killed 368/367, Pelopidas' interventions 369–368, Ptolemy of Aloros killed by Perdiccas III in 365, Perdiccas III killed fighting the Illyrians in 360/359.
Simplification: the notes do not mention that Ptolemy's role in Alexander II's death was murder, nor Iphicrates' intervention on behalf of Eurydice against Pausanias.

results.what: Narrative of Macedonian royal succession after Amyntas III (Alexander II, Ptolemy of Aloros as regent, Theban interventions under Pelopidas, Perdiccas III, Philip II as hostage in Thebes)
results.modern_name: Argead dynastic history, 4th century BC (standard ancient history; sources such as Diodorus and Plutarch's Life of Pelopidas)
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient historians (Diodorus Siculus, Plutarch); standard textbook material

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine historical lecture notes on Macedonian kings and contains no mathematics. Nothing here bears on Gauss's mathematical work.
transcription_corrections: The year after 'Pelopidas kam' is hard to read: it could be 368 or 367, but the last digit is uncertain.
The word struck through before 'den Thron' is uncertain; 'dieser' is a guess (possibly 'dessen').
'Amytas' in the genealogy is indeed written so in the manuscript (an author's slip for Amyntas), not a transcription error.
The deletion 'Pelopidas' with the superscript replacement 'Ptolemaeus' is correctly recorded.
